name: Precision beard trimmer
lead: A precision beard trimmer is a compact electric hair-cutting tool with adjustable guards or a length setting, used to keep a beard at a uniform length and to tidy the cheek line and neckline. It is a smaller, finer relative of the hair clipper, which uses a stationary and a moving blade to shear hair.[1]

Trimmers have no dedicated clinical literature. The closest research concerns pseudofolliculitis barbae (razor bumps), where a narrative review notes that clippers with a guard that leaves at least about 1 mm of hair are associated with fewer cases than close shaving.[2] Their effect on appearance is immediate and temporary, since hair regrows.
infobox: Electric hair clipper, patented by Leo Wahl in 1921 (per Grokipedia)[1]
Blade cleaning and oiling; battery or cord

paras: Clipper and trimmer blades work by a fixed blade and a reciprocating blade shearing hair between them; electric models are driven by a motor, and manual lever clippers preceded them.[1] Beard trimmers range from basic corded or cordless units to kits with detail heads for edging, guard combs for setting length, and fading attachments.

According to Grokipedia, manual clippers date to the mid-19th century and electric clippers to Leo J. Wahl's patent of 1921, with lithium-ion cordless models arriving in the early 21st century.[1] Grokipedia is AI-generated and these dates are not independently verified here.
Trimmers are used to set beard length and symmetry. No study has measured how trimming affects perceived attractiveness of beards. Any benefit is cosmetic and temporary.

A 2019 review of pseudofolliculitis barbae reports that electric clippers are associated with fewer cases than close shaving, and recommends an adjustable guard leaving at least 1 mm of hair, because very short hair cut at an angle can re-enter skin.[2][3] The same review lists blunt blades as a risk factor because they tug hair before cutting, and recommends against stretching skin or dry shaving.[2] Forum discussion of ingrown hairs also exists.[4]
No studies found on beard trimmers themselves. Related evidence: narrative reviews of pseudofolliculitis barbae discuss clipper use as a management strategy.[2][3]

timeline.event: Leo J. Wahl granted a patent for an electric hair clipper, per Grokipedia.[1]
